docs.title: A Parquet lakehouse with DuckDB
docs.text: Turn a folder of 835 files into partitioned Parquet that any engine can query. All of it is SQL in DuckDB with the oxedi extension (see DuckDB to install it).

docs.title: Read a folder
docs.text:
read_835 takes a path, a glob or a list. Add filename := true to know which file each row came from. Row numbers restart in every file, so a child table joins its parent on the file name and the row number.

SELECT filename, count(*) AS claims, sum(payment_amount) AS paid
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'claims', filename := true)
GROUP BY filename
ORDER BY filename;

docs.title: Write Parquet partitioned by payer and month
docs.text:
One wide table of claims, with the payer and the payment date from the payment each claim belongs to, is the usual starting point.

CREATE TABLE claims_wide AS
SELECT
    p.payer_name                              AS payer,
    strftime(p.payment_date, '%Y-%m')         AS month,
    p.trace_number,
    c.claim_id,
    c.claim_status,
    c.charge_amount,
    c.payment_amount,
    c.patient_responsibility,
    c.filename
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'claims', filename := true) c
JOIN read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'payments', filename := true) p
  ON p.filename = c.filename AND p."row" = c.payment;

COPY claims_wide TO 'claims_lake' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (payer, month), OVERWRITE_OR_IGNORE);

The output has one folder per payer and month, such as claims_lake/payer=ACME%20HEALTH%20PLAN/month=2024-01/ (values are URL-encoded). Read it back, with the partition values as columns:

SELECT payer, month, count(*) AS claims, sum(payment_amount) AS paid
FROM read_parquet('claims_lake/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true)
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY ALL;

Do the same for services and adjustments and join them on filename and the row references, as in the query above.

docs.title: Use diagnostics as a quality gate
docs.text:
Every file parses, and its problems come back as rows of the diagnostics table. Count them before you publish a batch. ignore_errors := true turns a file that is not an 835 into a row, so one bad file does not stop the run.

SELECT filename, level, rule, count(*) AS findings
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'diagnostics', filename := true, ignore_errors := true)
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY filename, level;

An empty result means the batch is clean. To stop a script at the first problem, make the count fail the statement:

SELECT CASE WHEN count(*) = 0 THEN 'clean'
            ELSE error('835 diagnostics found: ' || count(*)) END AS gate
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'diagnostics', ignore_errors := true);

docs.title: dbt sources over read_835
docs.text:
With dbt-duckdb, load the extension in the profile and build one staging model per table. The profile (not executed here):

oxedi_lake:
  target: dev
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: duckdb
      path: lake.duckdb
      extensions:
        - name: oxedi
          repo: community

A staging model, models/staging/stg_claims.sql:

{{ config(materialized='view') }}

SELECT *
FROM read_835('{{ var("remits_glob", "remits/*.835") }}', table_name := 'claims', filename := true)

A dbt singular test fails when it returns rows, so a test that selects the diagnostics fails the build on any finding:

-- tests/no_835_diagnostics.sql: a dbt singular test passes when it returns no rows
SELECT *
FROM read_835('{{ var("remits_glob", "remits/*.835") }}', table_name := 'diagnostics', filename := true)

The same two statements without the template, which is what dbt sends to DuckDB:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW stg_claims AS
SELECT *
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'claims', filename := true);

SELECT count(*) AS claims, sum(payment_amount) AS paid FROM stg_claims;

SELECT *
FROM read_835('remits/*.835', table_name := 'diagnostics', filename := true);

docs.title: oxedi in a pipeline
docs.text: A pipeline step that receives an 835, checks it and hands it on needs four moves: parse the bytes, look at the diagnostics, keep or reject, and write the result out.

docs.title: The step
docs.text:
import oxedi
from pathlib import Path


def process(data: bytes, out_dir: Path, name: str) -> list:
    """Parse one file; write its tables as Parquet; return its findings."""
    try:
        result = oxedi.parse(data)
    except oxedi.ParseError as error:  # not an 835 at all
        return [str(error)]

    findings = [str(d) for d in result.diagnostics]
    if findings:
        return findings  # leave the file for a person; write nothing

    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for table in result.tables.keys():
        result.tables[table].to_polars().write_parquet(out_dir / f"{name}-{table}.parquet")
    return []


problems = process(Path("remittance.835").read_bytes(), Path("out"), "remittance")
print("clean" if not problems else problems)

parse never raises on questionable data, only on a file that is not an 835. Diagnostics are the signal. To triage, filter on level (the SNIP level) or rule. See Diagnostics.

The step has no global state and no I/O of its own beyond what you pass in, so it runs the same in a script, a task or a consumer.

docs.title: Keep the original bytes
docs.text:
A parsed file writes back exactly as it came in. Archive that alongside the tables, so the source of every number is one call away:

result = oxedi.parse_file("remittance.835")
assert result.document.write() == Path("remittance.835").read_bytes()

docs.title: Airflow
docs.text:
Wrap process in a task. Pass paths, not bytes, between tasks. Not executed here, because it needs an Airflow installation:

from airflow.sdk import task  # Airflow 2: from airflow.decorators import task

@task
def load_remittance(path: str) -> list:
    return process(Path(path).read_bytes(), Path("/data/out"), Path(path).stem)

docs.title: Dagster
docs.text:
An asset with the findings as metadata. Not executed here, because it needs Dagster:

from dagster import Config, Output, asset

class RemitConfig(Config):
    path: str

@asset
def remittance_tables(context, config: RemitConfig):
    path = config.path
    findings = process(Path(path).read_bytes(), Path("/data/out"), Path(path).stem)
    return Output(None, metadata={"findings": len(findings)})

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text: Treat each message as one file: call process on the message value and send a message with findings to a dead-letter topic when the list is not empty. Commit the offset only after the output is written, so a crash re-processes the message rather than losing it. oxedi.stream(data) yields one transaction at a time when a single message is large.

docs.title: Alongside SQL
docs.text: If the files land in object storage, the same checks run in DuckDB without Python. See a Parquet lakehouse.

docs.title: Analytics with Polars
docs.text: Read a folder of remittances into Polars frames and answer the usual questions: who denies, which adjustments cost the most, how charges compare with payments.

docs.title: Load a folder
docs.text:
Tables join across a file by row number, and row numbers restart in each file, so add the file name to every frame and join on it. Text columns are bytes in the tables. Cast them to String where you want to read or group by them.

from pathlib import Path

import oxedi
import polars as pl

parts = {}
for path in sorted(Path("remits").glob("*.835")):
    result = oxedi.parse_file(path)
    for name in result.tables.keys():
        frame = result.tables[name].to_polars().with_columns(file=pl.lit(path.name))
        parts.setdefault(name, []).append(frame)

tables = {name: pl.concat(frames) for name, frames in parts.items()}

payments = tables["payments"].select(
    "file", payment=pl.col("row"), payer=pl.col("payer_name").cast(pl.String)
)
claims = tables["claims"].join(payments, on=["file", "payment"])

claims now has the payer on every row.

docs.title: Denials by payer
docs.text:
Claim status 4 is a denial. Count them next to the total.

denials = claims.group_by("payer").agg(
    claims=pl.len(),
    denied=(pl.col("claim_status") == b"4").sum(),
    denied_charges=pl.col("charge_amount").filter(pl.col("claim_status") == b"4").sum(),
)
print(denials.with_columns(rate=pl.col("denied") / pl.col("claims")).sort("rate", descending=True))

docs.title: CO and PR adjustments
docs.text:
An adjustment belongs to a claim (when service is empty) or to one service line. Its group_code says who bears the amount: CO contractual obligation, PR patient responsibility, OA other adjustment, PI payer-initiated reduction (and CR correction, in 4010 files). Join the claims to get the payer, then total by group and reason.

adjustments = tables["adjustments"].join(
    claims.select("file", "payer", claim=pl.col("row")), on=["file", "claim"]
)

by_group = (
    adjustments.with_columns(
        group=pl.col("group_code").cast(pl.String),
        reason=pl.col("reason_code").cast(pl.String),
    )
    .group_by("payer", "group", "reason")
    .agg(amount=pl.col("amount").sum(), adjustments=pl.len())
    .sort("amount", descending=True)
)
print(by_group.filter(pl.col("group").is_in(["CO", "PR"])))

docs.title: Charged versus paid
docs.text:
Money columns are exact decimals, so sums do not drift.

summary = claims.group_by("payer").agg(
    charged=pl.col("charge_amount").sum(),
    paid=pl.col("payment_amount").sum(),
    patient=pl.col("patient_responsibility").sum(),
)
print(summary.with_columns(paid_share=(pl.col("paid").cast(pl.Float64) / pl.col("charged").cast(pl.Float64)).round(3)))

For large folders, use oxedi.stream per file to keep memory bounded. See Reading large files. When the data already lives in DuckDB or Parquet, see a Parquet lakehouse and read the result with pl.read_parquet.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The terms these pages use, in plain language. For a walk through a real file, read The 835 in five minutes.

docs.title: Interchange
docs.text: The outer envelope of a file, from ISA to IEA. It names the sender and the receiver, the date and time, and carries a control number. It holds one or more functional groups. oxedi.write produces one interchange.

docs.title: Functional group
docs.text: A group of transactions inside an interchange, from GS to GE. GS08 names the version of the format, such as 005010X221A1.

docs.title: Transaction set
docs.text: One 835, from ST to SE. Also called a transaction. In an 835 it is one payment, so it is one row of payments. oxedi.stream yields one batch per transaction.

docs.title: Segment
docs.text: One record of the file: an id such as CLP, then its elements, then the segment terminator (~ by default). Every byte of a file belongs to exactly one segment, which is how oxedi writes a file back unchanged.

docs.title: Element
docs.text: One value inside a segment. Elements are separated by the element separator (* by default) and numbered from 1, so CLP02 is the second element of CLP.

docs.title: Component
docs.text: One part of a composite element. Components are separated by the component separator (: by default). SVC01-2 is the second component of the first element of SVC, as in SVC*HC:99213.

docs.title: Delimiters
docs.text: The characters that split a file: element separator, component separator, segment terminator, and the optional repetition separator and release character. A file declares them in its ISA segment, and oxedi reads them from there.

docs.title: Qualifier
docs.text: An element that says what the next value means. N1*PR is the payer and N1*PE the payee. DTM*232 is a statement start date. The docs write a segment with its qualifier this way.

docs.title: Loop
docs.text: A group of segments that repeats together, named by the implementation guide: 1000A (the payer), 1000B (the payee), 2000 (a group of claims), 2100 (a claim), 2110 (a service line). A diagnostic's path names the open loops, with the instance number: 2100#2 is the second claim.

docs.title: Implementation guide
docs.text: The published rules for using the 835 in health care: which segments, loops, elements and codes a file has. The 5010 guide is 005010X221A1 and the 4010 guide 004010X091A1.

docs.title: Spec
docs.text: oxedi's description of the format, in JSON: loops, segments, elements, code lists, balancing rules and the tables to fill. oxedi ships a 5010 and a 4010 spec, and you can patch them. See Customizing the spec.

docs.title: Control number
docs.text: A number that must match between a header and its trailer: ISA13 and IEA02, GS06 and GE02, ST02 and SE02. The trailers also carry counts (SE01, GE01, IEA01), so a receiver can check that nothing is missing.

docs.title: 5010 and 4010
docs.text: The two versions of the 835 that oxedi reads and writes. 5010 is the default. A file declares its version in ISA12 and GS08.

docs.title: ERA
docs.text: Electronic remittance advice: another name for the 835.

docs.title: Payer
docs.text: Who pays: usually a health plan. It sends the 835. Its loop is 1000A, opened by N1*PR.

docs.title: Payee
docs.text: Who is paid: usually the provider that sent the claims. It receives the 835. Its loop is 1000B, opened by N1*PE.

docs.title: Check and EFT
docs.text: The two usual ways the money moves: a paper check, or an electronic funds transfer (EFT). The money travels apart from the 835. BPR04 holds the payment method as a code, such as CHK or ACH.

docs.title: Trace number
docs.text: TRN02, the check or EFT trace number. It lets the payee match the 835 to the money it received. It is the trace_number column of payments.

docs.title: Claim
docs.text: A request for payment the provider sent for some care. In the 835, each claim is a CLP segment and its loop 2100, and one row of claims.

docs.title: Claim status
docs.text: CLP02, a code for how the payer processed the claim. The 5010 spec lists ten codes. The Polars recipe counts status 4 as a denial.

docs.title: Service line
docs.text: One billed procedure or service of a claim: an SVC segment and its loop 2110, and one row of services.

docs.title: Adjustment
docs.text: A reason the paid amount differs from the billed one, with its amount: a CAS segment on a claim or on a service line. Each reason in a CAS is one row of adjustments.

docs.title: Group code
docs.text: CAS01, who bears an adjustment: CO contractual obligation, PR patient responsibility, OA other adjustment, PI payer-initiated reduction, and CR correction in 4010 files.

docs.title: CARC
docs.text: Claim adjustment reason code: the reason of an adjustment, in CAS02, CAS05 and so on. It is the reason_code column of adjustments. The codes come from an external code list whose texts are licensed, so these pages do not reproduce them. Look a code up in the official list.

docs.title: RARC
docs.text: Remittance advice remark code: a remark that adds detail to an adjustment, also from an external, licensed code list. In the 835 they sit in LQ (on a service line) and in MIA and MOA (on a claim). The built-in tables have no column for them. The segments stay in the document, and a spec patch can add a column.

docs.title: Provider adjustment
docs.text: An amount added to or taken from the whole payment, not from one claim: a PLB segment. Each adjustment in a PLB is one row of provider_adjustments.

docs.title: Balancing
docs.text: The amounts of an 835 must add up. A service line's charge minus its payment equals its adjustments. A claim's charge minus its payment equals its adjustments and those of its service lines. BPR02 equals the claims' payments minus the provider adjustments. A rule that fails is a level 3 diagnostic.

docs.title: Diagnostic
docs.text: One finding about the data of a file: the rule that failed, where, and the value. oxedi returns diagnostics as data instead of raising. See Diagnostics.

docs.title: SNIP level
docs.text:
The level a validation rule belongs to. oxedi reports three:

  • Level 1, integrity: envelopes, control numbers and counts, segment structure.
  • Level 2, requirements: required elements, types, lengths, codes and the loop structure.
  • Level 3, balancing: amounts that must add up.

docs.title: Document
docs.text: The file as oxedi holds it, indexed into segments and kept byte for byte. result.document.write() returns the file unchanged.

docs.title: Envelope
docs.text: What the writer needs besides the tables: sender, receiver, date, time and control number. In Python it is oxedi.Envelope. See Writing.

docs.title: Lossless
docs.text: Nothing in the file is dropped or changed. Unknown segments stay in the document, and a file writes back exactly as it was read.

docs.title: Segment ids
docs.text: Id Name What it holds in an 835 ISA Interchange control header Sender, receiver, date, time, version, control number and the delimiters. IEA Interchange control trailer The number of groups and the interchange control number. GS Functional group header Application sender and receiver, date, time, control number, version. GE Functional group trailer The number of transactions and the group control number. ST Transaction set header Starts one 835 and its control number. SE Transaction set trailer The number of segments and the transaction control number. BPR Financial information The total paid, credit or debit, method, format and date. TRN Reassociation trace number The trace number and the payer identifier. REF Reference identification An id, with a qualifier that says which one. DTM Date or time reference A date, with a qualifier that says which one. N1 Party identification The payer (N1*PR) or the payee (N1*PE): name and id. N3 Address A street address. N4 City, state and ZIP code City, state and postal code. PER Contact information A contact name and number. LX Header number Starts a group of claims (loop 2000). CLP Claim payment information A claim: id, status, charge, payment, patient responsibility. NM1 Individual or organization name A person or organization of the claim, such as the patient (NM1*QC). MIA, MOA Inpatient and outpatient adjudication information Adjudication amounts and remark codes of a claim. AMT Supplemental amount An amount, with a qualifier that says which one. SVC Service payment information A service line: procedure, charge, payment, units. CAS Claim or service adjustment Up to six adjustments of one group: reason, amount, quantity. LQ Health care remark codes Remark codes of a service line. PLB Provider adjustment Up to six adjustments of the whole payment.

docs.title: Tables and columns
docs.text:
oxedi reads every 835 into the same five tables. This page shows how they link and lists every column, with its type, the element it comes from and what it holds.

New to the 835? The 835 in five minutes explains payments, claims and adjustments first.

docs.title: How the tables link
docs.text:
erDiagram
    payments ||--o{ claims : "payment"
    payments ||--o{ provider_adjustments : "payment"
    claims ||--o{ services : "claim"
    claims ||--o{ adjustments : "claim"
    services ||--o{ adjustments : "service"
  • row numbers the rows of a table, from 0.
  • payment, claim and service hold the row of the parent.
  • A service joins to its claim on services.claim = claims.row.
  • An adjustment of a claim has a null service. An adjustment of a service line has the line's row in service.
  • Children also carry the row of every table above them. A service has both claim and payment.

Several files

Row numbers restart in every file. When you combine files, join on the file name as well as the row. The Polars and lakehouse recipes show how.

Details: row numbers in one file

row counts across the whole file, not per transaction. In a file with two payments, the claims of the second payment carry on from the last claim of the first.

docs.title: Columns every table has
docs.text:
Column Type Holds row int64 The row's number in its table, from 0. segment int64 The index of the segment the row starts at: its CLP for a claim, its CAS for an adjustment. result.document[segment] gives that segment. payment int64 The row of the payment the row belongs to. Not in payments. claim int64 The row of the claim. In services and adjustments. service int64 The row of the service line, or null for a claim adjustment. In adjustments.

The tables list these columns first and the others in name order.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
Type here Python (Arrow) Polars DuckDB text binary Binary VARCHAR (BLOB with binary := true) decimal(38, 2) decimal128(38, 2) Decimal(38, 2) DECIMAL(38,2) decimal(38, 4) decimal128(38, 4) Decimal(38, 4) DECIMAL(38,4) date date32 Date DATE int64 int64 Int64 BIGINT
  • Text keeps the bytes of the file. Cast to a string type to read or group by it.
  • A text element the segment does not have is null. One it has but leaves empty is "".
  • In the other types, a value that is missing, empty or does not parse is null. The parse reports a value that does not parse as a diagnostic.

docs.title: How to read the source column
docs.text:
• BPR02 is element 2 of the BPR segment.
  • SVC01-2 is component 2 of element 1 of SVC.
  • of NM1*QC means the NM1 segment whose first element is QC. A claim has several NM1 segments, and this one is the patient.
  • When a segment repeats where the table reads it, the column takes the first one.

The glossary explains each segment id. The spec defines all of this, and you can change it: see Customizing the spec.

docs.title: payments
docs.text:
One row per payment, which is one transaction (ST to SE). The payer is loop 1000A and the payee loop 1000B.

Column Type Source Holds handling_code text BPR01 The transaction handling code. total_payment_amount decimal(38, 2) BPR02 The total actual payment to the provider. credit_debit_flag text BPR03 Whether the amount is a credit (C) or a debit (D). payment_method text BPR04 The payment method code, such as CHK or ACH. payment_format text BPR05 The payment format code. payment_date date BPR16 The check issue date or the EFT effective date. trace_number text TRN02 The check or EFT trace number. payer_identifier text TRN03 The payer identifier of the trace. receiver_id text REF02 of REF*EV The receiver identification. production_date date DTM02 of DTM*405 The production date. payer_name text N102 of N1*PR The payer's name. payer_id_qualifier text N103 of N1*PR The kind of id in payer_id. payer_id text N104 of N1*PR The payer's identification code. payer_address text N301 in loop 1000A The payer's address. payer_city text N401 in loop 1000A The payer's city. payer_state text N402 in loop 1000A The payer's state or province code. payer_zip text N403 in loop 1000A The payer's postal code. payer_technical_contact_name text PER02 of PER*BL The name of the payer's technical contact. payer_technical_contact_qualifier text PER03 of PER*BL The kind of number in payer_technical_contact_number. payer_technical_contact_number text PER04 of PER*BL The technical contact's communication number. payee_name text N102 of N1*PE The payee's name. payee_id_qualifier text N103 of N1*PE The kind of id in payee_id. payee_id text N104 of N1*PE The payee's identification code. payee_address text N301 in loop 1000B The payee's address. payee_city text N401 in loop 1000B The payee's city. payee_state text N402 in loop 1000B The payee's state or province code. payee_zip text N403 in loop 1000B The payee's postal code.

4010 files

The 4010 spec has no payer technical contact (PER*BL), so on 4010 files the payer_technical_contact_* columns are usually null.

docs.title: claims
docs.text:
One row per claim (CLP, loop 2100).

Column Type Source Holds claim_id text CLP01 The claim submitter's identifier: the provider's id for the claim. claim_status text CLP02 The claim status code. See claim status. charge_amount decimal(38, 2) CLP03 The total charge of the claim. payment_amount decimal(38, 2) CLP04 The amount paid for the claim. patient_responsibility decimal(38, 2) CLP05 The patient responsibility amount. filing_indicator text CLP06 The claim filing indicator code. payer_control_number text CLP07 The payer's claim control number. facility_type text CLP08 The facility type code. frequency_code text CLP09 The claim frequency type code. drg_code text CLP11 The DRG code. drg_weight decimal(38, 4) CLP12 The DRG weight. discharge_fraction decimal(38, 4) CLP13 The discharge fraction. header_number int64 LX01 The number of the LX group (loop 2000) the claim is in. patient_last_name text NM103 of NM1*QC The patient's last name. patient_first_name text NM104 of NM1*QC The patient's first name. patient_id_qualifier text NM108 of NM1*QC The kind of id in patient_id. patient_id text NM109 of NM1*QC The patient's identification code. rendering_provider_entity_type text NM102 of NM1*82 The entity type qualifier of the service provider. rendering_provider_name text NM103 of NM1*82 The service provider's last or organization name. rendering_provider_id_qualifier text NM108 of NM1*82 The kind of id in rendering_provider_id. rendering_provider_id text NM109 of NM1*82 The service provider's identification code. statement_from date DTM02 of DTM*232 The first date of the claim's statement period. statement_to date DTM02 of DTM*233 The last date of the claim's statement period. coverage_amount decimal(38, 2) AMT02 of AMT*AU The coverage amount. group_number text REF02 of REF*1L The group number.

docs.title: services
docs.text:
One row per service line (SVC, loop 2110).

Column Type Source Holds procedure_qualifier text SVC01-1 The kind of code in procedure_code, such as HC. procedure_code text SVC01-2 The procedure or service code. charge_amount decimal(38, 2) SVC02 The line item charge. payment_amount decimal(38, 2) SVC03 The amount paid for the line. units_paid decimal(38, 2) SVC05 The units of service paid. original_units decimal(38, 2) SVC07 The original units of service. service_date date DTM02 of DTM*472 The service date. line_item_control_number text REF02 of REF*6R The line item control number. allowed_amount decimal(38, 2) AMT02 of AMT*B6 The allowed amount.

docs.title: adjustments
docs.text:
One row per adjustment. A CAS segment holds up to six adjustments of one group: the reason, amount and quantity of each sit in three elements in a row. Each becomes its own row.

Column Type Source Holds group_code text CAS01 The claim adjustment group code, such as CO or PR. See group code. reason_code text CAS02, CAS05, … The adjustment reason code (a CARC). amount decimal(38, 2) CAS03, CAS06, … The adjustment amount. quantity decimal(38, 2) CAS04, CAS07, … The adjustment quantity.

docs.title: provider_adjustments
docs.text:
One row per provider adjustment. A PLB segment holds up to six adjustments for one provider and fiscal period: an identifier and an amount each. Each becomes its own row.

Column Type Source Holds provider_id text PLB01 The provider identifier. fiscal_period_date date PLB02 The fiscal period date. reason_code text PLB03-1, PLB05-1, … The provider adjustment reason code. reference_id text PLB03-2, PLB05-2, … The reference identification of the adjustment. amount decimal(38, 2) PLB04, PLB06, … The provider adjustment amount.

Adjustments that share a segment came from the same PLB. The writer keeps them together, as Writing from your own tables explains.

docs.title: diagnostics (DuckDB only)
docs.text:
In DuckDB, read_835(..., table_name := 'diagnostics') returns the findings of the parse as a sixth table, one row per finding:

Column Type Holds level BIGINT The SNIP level of the rule: 1, 2 or 3. kind VARCHAR The name of the rule, such as CodeNotInList. rule VARCHAR The rule as a sentence with its values. segment BIGINT The index of the segment at fault. element, component BIGINT The 1-based position in the segment, when there is one. path VARCHAR The loops open at that segment. datum VARCHAR The offending value. origin, code VARCHAR Who reported it, and that reporter's own code.

In Python the same fields are on each oxedi.Diagnostic. See Diagnostics.

docs.title: See the columns of any table
docs.text:
The spec decides the columns, so a patched spec can add some. To list them:

PythonSQL 
import oxedi

result = oxedi.parse_file("remittance.835")
print(result.tables["services"].columns)

['row', 'segment', 'payment', 'claim', 'allowed_amount', 'charge_amount', 'line_item_control_number', 'original_units', 'payment_amount', 'procedure_code', 'procedure_qualifier', 'service_date', 'units_paid']

DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM read_835('remittance.835', table_name := 'services');

Without a file, ask the spec: Spec.schema() in Python and oxedi_schema() in SQL give each table's columns, types and references. See See the columns a table needs.

docs.text: Every transaction of the files parsed.

Every transaction's rows, with the numbered columns sorted last. The frames are concatenated one at a time onto an empty frame, as the library does, so empty transactions give the same dtypes. docs.title: parse
docs.text:
parse(
    path: Union[str, "os.PathLike[str]"],
    debug: bool = False,
) -> TransactionSets

Parses a file path, or every .txt, .835 and .DAT file of a directory, with the same signature and behaviour as edi_835_parser.parse. Data already in memory goes through parse_bytes, parse_file_obj or parse_many.

Beyond the library: any path-like (pathlib.Path) is accepted, "" raises FileNotFoundError where the library raises IndexError, and a file whose ISA cannot be read (with no byte order mark before it) raises ParseError naming the file where the library raises IndexError.

docs.title: parse_bytes
docs.text:
parse_bytes(

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(
    source: Source,
    mask: Optional[Mask] = None,
    spec: Optional[Spec] = None,
) -> list[Diagnostic]

Validates an 835 file with pyx12 and returns what it finds.

source is the file's bytes, a path, or a file object open in binary mode. pyx12 picks its map from the file's own version declaration. pyx12's own defaults apply: extended character set (charset="E"), no external code lists excluded (exclude_external_codes=None), and user/system configuration files (~/.pyx12.conf.xml, <prefix>/etc/pyx12.conf.xml) are not read, so findings do not depend on the machine.

Every error pyx12's engine records is returned: interchange, group and transaction errors, segment errors and element errors, including those of the envelope segments. They are read from the error tree pyx12 builds; pyx12's logging is not used. The pyx12 logger gets a logging.NullHandler the first time, when it has none, so pyx12's records are not printed by default and still reach the handlers the caller configures; levels, propagation and logging.disable stay as the caller set them.

Each finding is an oxedi.Diagnostic, the type parse returns, so both lists mix, sort by level and filter by origin. A pyx12 finding has kind == "External", origin == "pyx12" and code set to pyx12's own error code; rule is pyx12's message. level follows where pyx12 reports it: interchange, group and transaction findings are level 1, segment and element findings level 2. segment is the index of the segment at fault in the file's document (None when pyx12 names none), and document[d.segment].span gives its byte range. An interchange, group or transaction finding about a trailer (a count or a control number that does not match) lands on the trailer segment at the element holding that value; one about a duplicate or missing control structure lands on the header, at its control number when that is the offending value. datum is the value pyx12 reports, or else the bytes of the element in the file, or the segment id for a finding with no element. Findings come in segment order. path names the loops open at that segment, as in the diagnostics parse gives about the same segment.

A file pyx12 cannot read, or an exception inside pyx12, gives one level 1 finding with no code whose rule starts with could not finish validating, instead of raising: a file pyx12 rejects points at the segment holding the ISA with its bytes as the datum; a failure while reading names the segment pyx12 was processing, and one after the last segment names the last segment it completed. A file with no ISA to read the delimiters from raises oxedi.ParseError, as oxedi.parse does. Nothing is written to disk and no acknowledgement is generated.

With mask, an oxedi.Mask, the datum of a finding at a place a column flags as patient data reads is masked as parse masks its own diagnostics with that mask. In the finding's message, the original datum and each value its segment holds at such a place are replaced by their masked forms, whether or not the finding names an element. A value of 4 characters or more is replaced wherever it occurs. A shorter one is replaced only where it stands apart: the character on each side is the edge of the message, a character that is not an ASCII letter or digit (an accented letter or - counts), or part of another replaced value. Short values that overlap or touch are replaced as one group when the group stands apart. A short value glued to letters or digits that are not flagged values stays as written (with XAB and ABYZ flagged, QXABYZ keeps QX), and two short values that together spell a word of the message replace that word. Every other attribute, and the findings' number and order, stay as without it. The flagged places are those of the spec the parse uses: spec, an oxedi.Spec, or the built-in spec of the file's version when it is None, so a patched spec that flags more columns masks them here as parse(source, spec=spec, mask=mask) does. The same spec locates the findings' loop paths, as in parse(source, spec=spec). A failure finding for an exception inside pyx12, whose text no flagged place points at, keeps the exception's type and drops its text: could not finish validating: ValueError, whose message is not shown with a mask; ..., or its error tree could not be read (ValueError, whose message is not shown with a mask). The rest of such a finding is text oxedi wrote, so the mask does not rewrite it; its datum is masked as any other. The finding for a file pyx12 rejects quotes pyx12's X12Error, which can hold the whole ISA line, and its message is masked as pyx12's messages are; its datum is ISA instead of the ISA line, which names no element. pyx12 still reads the original file: the mask hides what validate returns, not what pyx12 is given. mask of any other type than oxedi.Mask or None raises TypeError, and so does spec of any other type than oxedi.Spec or None.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
In five minutes you will parse a remittance file, see what it paid, find one problem in it and write it back byte for byte. You need Python 3.11 or later.

New to the 835?

An 835 is the file a health plan sends to a provider to explain a payment. The 835 in five minutes explains the format. You can read it before or after this page.

docs.title: Install oxedi
docs.text:
pip install "oxedi[polars]"

This installs oxedi with Polars, which the examples use to show tables. Plain pip install oxedi has no Python dependencies at all. Install lists every extra and platform.

docs.title: Get the example file
docs.text:
The examples read a small file named remittance.835. It holds one payment of 690.00 from ACME HEALTH PLAN to SUNRISE CLINIC, covering four claims. Download it into your working directory:

curl -o remittance.835 https://raw.githubusercontent.com/javillegasna/oxedi/master/crates/oxedi_core/tests/fixtures/balanced_5010_sample.txt

docs.title: Parse the file
docs.text:
import oxedi

result = oxedi.parse_file("remittance.835")

print(result)
print(result.count_claims(), result.sum_payments())
print(result.payer["name"], "paid", result.payee["name"])

Result(segments=63, tables=5, diagnostics=0)
4 690.00
ACME HEALTH PLAN paid SUNRISE CLINIC

The file has 63 segments, the lines of an 835. oxedi read them into five tables and found no problems. sum_payments() is a Decimal, so money is exact.

docs.title: Look at the claims
docs.text:
The five tables are ready to use:

print(result.tables)

Tables(adjustments: 15 rows, claims: 4 rows, payments: 1 rows, provider_adjustments: 3 rows, services: 4 rows)

Open the claims in Polars:

import polars as pl

claims = result.tables["claims"].to_polars().with_columns(pl.col(pl.Binary).cast(pl.String))
print(claims.select("row", "claim_id", "claim_status", "charge_amount", "payment_amount"))

┌─────┬──────────┬──────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐
│ row ┆ claim_id ┆ claim_status ┆ charge_amount ┆ payment_amount │
│ --- ┆ ---      ┆ ---          ┆ ---           ┆ ---            │
│ i64 ┆ str      ┆ str          ┆ decimal[38,2] ┆ decimal[38,2]  │
╞═════╪══════════╪══════════════╪═══════════════╪════════════════╡
│ 0   ┆ CLM1001  ┆ 1            ┆ 300.00        ┆ 200.00         │
│ 1   ┆ CLM1002  ┆ 2            ┆ 700.00        ┆ 400.00         │
│ 2   ┆ CLM2001  ┆ 1            ┆ 150.00        ┆ 120.00         │
│ 3   ┆ CLM2002  ┆ 4            ┆ 80.00         ┆ 0.00           │
└─────┴──────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘
  • Each row is one claim the provider sent to the payer.
  • charge_amount is what the provider billed. payment_amount is what the payer paid.
  • Claim status 4 is a denial: CLM2002 billed 80.00 and got nothing.

Why the cast to String?

oxedi keeps text exactly as the file has it, as raw bytes, so nothing is lost to an encoding guess. Cast to String when you want to read or group by text.

docs.title: See why a claim was paid less
docs.text:
CLM1001 billed 300.00 and was paid 200.00. The adjustments explain the difference. They link to their claim through the claim column, which holds the claim's row:

adjustments = result.tables["adjustments"].to_polars().with_columns(pl.col(pl.Binary).cast(pl.String))
print(adjustments.filter(pl.col("claim") == 0).select("service", "group_code", "reason_code", "amount"))

┌─────────┬────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┐
│ service ┆ group_code ┆ reason_code ┆ amount        │
│ ---     ┆ ---        ┆ ---         ┆ ---           │
│ i64     ┆ str        ┆ str         ┆ decimal[38,2] │
╞═════════╪════════════╪═════════════╪═══════════════╡
│ 0       ┆ PR         ┆ 1           ┆ 30.00         │
│ 0       ┆ CO         ┆ 45          ┆ 20.00         │
│ 1       ┆ PR         ┆ 2           ┆ 20.00         │
│ 1       ┆ PR         ┆ 3           ┆ 10.00         │
│ 1       ┆ CO         ┆ 45          ┆ 20.00         │
└─────────┴────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┘
  • The five adjustments add up to 100.00, the gap between 300.00 and 200.00.
  • group_code says who bears the amount: PR is patient responsibility, CO a contractual obligation.
  • reason_code is a claim adjustment reason code (CARC). See the glossary.
  • service says which service line of the claim each adjustment belongs to.

Tables and columns describes every table and column.

docs.title: Read a diagnostic
docs.text:
The example file is clean, so result.diagnostics is empty. To see a diagnostic, change one claim status to 7, a code the spec does not list, and parse again:

from pathlib import Path

data = Path("remittance.835").read_bytes()
broken = oxedi.parse(data.replace(b"CLP*CLM1002*2*", b"CLP*CLM1002*7*"))

for diagnostic in broken.diagnostics:
    print(diagnostic)

SNIP 2 · element CLP02 (claim_status_code) is not one of the 10 codes the spec lists for it · segment #36, element 2 · at interchange#1/group#1/transaction#1/2000#1/2100#2 · datum "7"

Read it from left to right:

  • SNIP 2: the level of the rule. Level 2 covers required elements, types, lengths and codes.
  • The rule that failed, with the element (CLP02, the claim status).
  • Where: the segment at index 36 of the file (counting from 0), element 2.
  • The loops open at that point: the second claim (2100#2) of the first transaction.
  • datum: the value that broke the rule, 7.

The parse did not stop. The claim is still in broken.tables, with its status 7. To see the segment itself, index the document with the diagnostic's segment:

segment = broken.document[broken.diagnostics[0].segment]
print(segment.raw)

b'\nCLP*CLM1002*7*700*400*0*12*PCN1002*11*1~'

Diagnostics lists every kind of finding and what to do about it.

docs.title: Write the file back
docs.text:
oxedi keeps every byte of the file, so the document writes it back unchanged:

assert result.document.write() == data

To build a new file from tables instead, use oxedi.write. Writing shows how.

The base package has no Python dependencies. Add an extra for the library you work with:

Install Adds Use it to pip install "oxedi[polars]" Polars get tables as Polars frames pip install "oxedi[pandas]" pandas and pyarrow get tables as pandas frames pip install "oxedi[pyx12]" pyx12 validate with pyx12 pip install "oxedi[edi-835-parser]" a drop-in layer keep code written for edi-835-parser

You can combine extras: pip install "oxedi[polars,pyx12]".

docs.title: The 835 in five minutes
docs.text: This page explains what an 835 file is, how it is built and how oxedi turns it into tables. You do not need to know X12 to follow it. The glossary defines every term.

docs.title: What an 835 is
docs.text:
A provider (a clinic, a hospital, a doctor) sends claims to a health plan to be paid for the care it gave. The health plan pays, usually in one payment that covers many claims. The 835 tells the provider what that payment covers.

  • Its full name is the X12 835 Health Care Claim Payment/Advice. It is also called an electronic remittance advice (ERA).
  • The payer (the health plan) sends it. The payee (the provider) receives it.
  • The money itself moves separately, by check or by electronic funds transfer (EFT). The 835 carries a trace number so the provider can match the file to the money.
  • For each claim it says what was billed, what was paid and why the two differ.

oxedi reads the 5010 version of the format (005010X221A1) and the older 4010 version (004010X091A1).

docs.title: How a payment breaks down
docs.text:
An 835 nests from the payment down to single adjustments:

flowchart TD
    P["Payment<br/>BPR, TRN: amount, method, date, trace number<br/>N1: payer and payee"]
    C["Claim<br/>CLP: billed, paid, patient's share, status"]
    S["Service line<br/>SVC: procedure, billed, paid"]
    CA["Claim adjustment<br/>CAS: group, reason, amount"]
    SA["Service adjustment<br/>CAS: group, reason, amount"]
    PA["Provider adjustment<br/>PLB: reason, amount"]
    P --> C
    P --> PA
    C --> S
    C --> CA
    S --> SA
  • Payment. One per transaction. It holds the total paid, how and when, and who pays whom.
  • Claim. One per claim the provider sent. A payment covers one or more claims.
  • Service line. One per procedure or service billed on the claim. A claim may have none.
  • Adjustment. A reason why the paid amount differs from the billed one. It sits on a claim or on one of its service lines.
  • Provider adjustment. An amount added to or taken from the whole payment, not from one claim.

The money balances at every level. A service line's billed amount minus its paid amount equals the sum of its adjustments. A claim's billed minus paid equals the sum of its own adjustments and those of its service lines. The payment's total equals the claims' payments minus the provider adjustments. oxedi checks these rules and reports a diagnostic when one fails.

docs.title: How oxedi maps it to tables
docs.text:
Each level becomes one table. Each row points to its parent by the parent's row number.

Table One row per Points to its parent with payments payment none claims claim payment services service line payment, claim adjustments claim or service adjustment payment, claim, service (empty on a claim adjustment) provider_adjustments provider adjustment payment

Tables and columns shows every column and the element it comes from.

docs.title: What the file looks like
docs.text:
An 835 is plain text. Each line here is a segment, ending with ~. The first word is the segment's id. The values after it are its elements, separated by *. Some elements hold components, separated by :.

Opens a row of payments BPR*I*690*C*CHK…*20240112 690.00 paid by check (CHK), dated 2024-01-12. total_payment_amount, payment_method, payment_date TRN*1*CHK100234*1512345678 The trace number that matches the money. trace_number, payer_identifier N1*PR*ACME HEALTH PLAN The payer (PR), with its address in N3 and N4. payer_name, payer_address, payer_city, … N1*PE*SUNRISE CLINIC*XX*1234567893 The payee (PE), with its id and the id's qualifier XX. payee_name, payee_id_qualifier, payee_id LX*1 A group of claims starts. header_number of each claim CLP*CLM1001*1*300*200*60… Claim CLM1001, status 1: billed 300, paid 200, patient owes 60. A row of claims NM1*QC*1*DOE*JANE…*MI*MBR0001 The patient (QC) and the patient's member id. patient_last_name, patient_first_name, patient_id DTM*232*20240105 The claim's statement period starts (232). statement_from SVC*HC:99213*200*150**1 A service line: procedure 99213 (qualifier HC), billed 200, paid 150, 1 unit paid. A row of services CAS*PR*1*30 An adjustment of the service: group PR, reason 1, 30.00. A row of adjustments AMT*B6*180 The allowed amount of the service line. allowed_amount

The envelope wraps the transaction. ISA and GS come before ST. SE, GE and IEA close them in reverse order. They carry who sent the file, when, and the counts and control numbers that let the receiver check nothing is missing.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
The implementation guide groups segments into loops, named by number. oxedi uses those names in diagnostics and in the spec:

Loop Starts with Holds 1000A N1*PR the payer 1000B N1*PE the payee 2000 LX a group of claims 2100 CLP one claim 2110 SVC one service line

PLB and the payment segments (BPR, TRN) belong to the transaction itself, outside any numbered loop.

docs.title: Try it in your browser
docs.text: You can read an 835 file without installing anything. Open the oxedi viewer, drop a file on it and look at the payment, the tables and the problems oxedi found.

docs.title: Open a file
docs.text:
1. Open https://javillegas.dev/oxedi/viewer/.
  2. Drop an 835 file on the page, or click it to choose one. The file can have any extension.
  3. Press Try the sample if you only want to look around. The sample is a small synthetic file.

If the file is not an 835, the page shows the parser's message and keeps working, so you can drop the next file.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
The viewer runs the same parser as the Python package, compiled to WebAssembly. A file opens in five views:

View What it shows Summary The payer, the payee, the payment method, the date, the total and the counts. Tables Payments, claims, service lines and adjustments. You can filter the rows and download them as CSV. Diagnostics Each problem oxedi found, with the rule, the position and the value. Text The original file, one segment per line. Loops The loop structure, which you can fold.

Tick Hide patient data to replace the patient's name, ids and dates with tokens and years. The tables, the diagnostics and the CSV export show the masked values; the Text and Loops views still show the original file, so do not share a screenshot of them. The key is random, made when the page loads and never leaves it, so tokens match within one visit only. Untick it to see the original values again.

A diagnostic links to its segment in the Text view, with the element it names highlighted. A segment cell in a table does the same. Every byte of the file is shown, including line breaks after a terminator and a last segment that has none.

Summary also shows which version of the spec the page used, 5010 or 4010, chosen from the file.

docs.title: Your file stays on your machine
docs.text:
The page has no server behind it. It reads the file in your browser and never sends it anywhere. It also asks the browser to forbid network connections, so even a bug could not send the file out.

Check it yourself
  1. Open the browser's developer tools and go to the Network tab.
  2. Drop a file on the page.
  3. No request appears after the page has loaded.

The page carries a Content-Security-Policy with connect-src 'none', which you can read in the page's source. It uses no analytics and no third-party fonts or scripts.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It only reads. It does not edit or write an 835.
  • It opens one file at a time.
  • It does not validate with pyx12, which is a Python library. Use the Python package for that.

Large files

A file over 20 MB makes the page ask before it parses. The largest sample in the repository, about 600 KB with 30 000 segments, opens in well under a second on a laptop.
